transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Louise Schiavone, a big shake up in the tech sector
today and on Wall Street as chip giant Nvidia reinstated controversial president and CEO
Jensen Wong.
President Trump has been outspoken about getting Wong back in charge following his resignation
on news of multiple affairs, particularly with a woman suspected of spying for the Chinese
government which raised concerns about national security.
The latest development led Wall Street to recover about half of last week's losses,
but the good economic news was not persuasive enough to assuage concerns of lawmakers about
Wong's fitness for the job, and PR's Katie McHugh has more.
It's not just about Wong himself.
Doctors are also asking whether Nvidia shared sensitive information or technology with Chinese
interests.
Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren calls the decision to reappoint Wong reckless.
She says Nvidia's board still owes Congress answers about its compliance with export controls.
Republican Don Bacon called for Congress to investigate who approved the licenses that
will allow Nvidia to export high-end AI chips to Chinese customers.
President Trump told CNBC he personally made the deal with Nvidia's board to engineer
Wong's comeback, and Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego wants to investigate whether members
of the White House were involved in any stock trades before the Nvidia announcement.
Katie McHugh, NPR News, New York.
President Trump has stopped a controversial plan to blow up five tons of bomb-making materials
at an Iowa ammunition plant, and PR's Franco Ordonez reports.
The blast was initially planned for Friday, but as plans became public, nearby residents
began to raise concerns, and an environmental review found that dust from even a controlled
explosion could contain toxic elements, such as lead.
President Trump said he still feels the proper course is to get rid of the hazardous materials,
but he ordered the stand-down until a federal court weighs in, as well as the incoming governor.
Trump said he would move forward if the courts and governor-elect Rob Sand disagree, but that
he would hold Sand responsible for any "death or destruction" caused by the situation.
The Army has warned that the risk of accidental explosion will increase as temperatures drop,
Franco Ordonez, NPR News.
The AAA expects 81 million Americans to mark the Thanksgiving holiday with some kind of
travel.
Nearly 6 million of them will fly.
Stormy, late autumn weather is in store across the nation on the West Coast.
A confluence of two things could bring flooding, rain fueled by wide bands of moisture, and
king tides expected to be among the highest tides this year.
Western Oklahoma, Texas, the Great Lakes, and New England could see some snow.
Heavy wind and rain are possible in the southeast and along the east coast.
Wall Street today, the Dow was up 1,447 points.
The S&P's 500 picked up 326.
This is NPR.
Ringpiece Middle East is reporting the war in Iran has caused more than 600 oil slicks
in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters.
Natural habitats for plants and wildlife, as well as soil quality and food chains, are
under significant pressure.
Families of young children say their kids are kind even as they overwhelmingly see the
world as an unkind place.
According to a big new survey from Sesame Workshop, NPR's Corey Turner has details.
The education nonprofit behind Sesame Street has twice surveyed American families about
kindness in 2016 and now a decade later.
And the differences are striking.
This national sample of caregivers of kids ages 3 to 8 saw a big increase in families
who say kindness is just not a priority for most people.
And they gave Americans a pretty middling rating for kindness, 2.8 out of 5.
But compared to a decade ago, kids earned higher marks for kindness and resilience and
they were less likely to be considered anxious.
Caregivers themselves were also much more likely in 2026 to say they value empathy in
their kids over manners.
Corey Turner, NPR News.
Huge Super Bowl fans will have an opportunity to see the big game this February live on
a huge IMAX screen.
Walt Disney, ESPN, and the National Football League are partnering with IMAX with this
project.
Hundreds of IMAX locations will participate across the U.S. and in other countries including
Australia, New Zealand, and Brazil.
I'm Louise Givone, NPR News, Washington.

topics.text: Nvidia reinstates CEO Jensen Huang after resignation over affairs and national security concerns
Lawmakers including Warren and Bacon question Nvidia's board and chip export licenses to China
Trump halts controlled explosion of five tons of bomb-making materials at Iowa ammunition plant
AAA expects 81 million Americans to travel for Thanksgiving; stormy West Coast weather forecast
Dow jumps 1,447 points as Wall Street recovers about half of last week's losses
Iran war causes more than 600 oil slicks in Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters
Sesame Workshop survey finds families see world as unkind though children rate kindness higher
Super Bowl to be shown live on IMAX screens in hundreds of locations worldwide
